sections.title: A small burnt-ground Gymnopilus
sections.text: Gymnopilus pseudofulgens Romagn. is a gilled mushroom in the family Hymenogastraceae. The name is retained by the taxonomic catalogues consulted. It is chiefly documented on burnt ground, sometimes among mosses and charcoal; it should not be depicted as a large cluster growing from a stump.

sections.title: Reddish-brown cap
sections.text: The cap is small, generally 8–22 mm wide, campanulate or conical at first, then conico-convex to convex, sometimes slightly umbonate. It is dark reddish brown and fades to a duller, paler rufous colour as it dries. Its surface is opaque and unstriated, and may look silky when dry.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are moderately crowded, rather broad and adnate, without a pronounced notch. They begin beige to yellowish and become yellow-rust, remaining relatively pale for a Gymnopilus. The slender, cylindrical stem is about 19–49 mm long and 1.5–3 mm wide, rufous and darker toward the base; it is initially pruinose, then becomes nearly glabrous. A veil was not observed in the original description.

sections.title: Habitat and distinction
sections.text: The species is described as carbonicolous: it occurs on burnt ground, often with mosses. A farinaceous, sometimes slightly bitter taste and ellipsoid to amygdaliform, finely verrucose spores are reported in descriptions; spores measure about 8.5–11.7 × 4.5–5.5 µm. Identification requires microscopy and comparison with other small carbonicolous Gymnopilus, including G. decipiens and G. fulgens.

traits: Small cap, 8–22 mm, conical or bell-shaped then convex, reddish brown and paling as it dries
Opaque, unstriated surface, sometimes silky when dry
Moderately crowded, adnate gills, beige-yellowish then yellow-rust
Slender stem, 19–49 × 1.5–3 mm, rufous and darker at the base, initially pruinose
Carbonicolous species documented on burnt ground, sometimes among mosses
Ellipsoid to amygdaliform, verrucose spores, about 8.5–11.7 × 4.5–5.5 µm
safetyNote: Edibility is not assessed here. Small Gymnopilus species can be difficult to distinguish; this entry and its illustration cannot identify a foraged specimen or establish that it is edible.
